1.o: We here find Ahaziah, the genuine son and successor of Ahab, on the throne of Israel. His reign continued not two years; he died by a fall in his own house, of which, after the mention of the revolt of Moab (ver. 1), we have here an account. I. The message which, on that occasion, he sent to the god of Ekron, ver. 2. II. The message he received from the God of Israel, ver. 3-8. III. The destruction of the messengers he sent to seize the prophet, once and again, ver. 9-12. IV.
1.i: Second Kings 1 follows an injured king who asks the wrong god for help, and the prophet who would not be arrested.
1.p: Lord, You alone are God of Israel. Keep us from running to false helpers, and teach us to come to You with humble hearts. Amen.
1.l: When you need help today, take your question to God first, before you ask anywhere else.
q: The second captain obeyed blindly. When has following orders without thinking put you in a bad place?

2.o: In this chapter we have, I. That extraordinary event, the translation of Elijah. In the close of the foregoing chapter we had a wicked king leaving the world in disgrace, here we have a holy prophet leaving it in honour; the departure of the former was his greatest misery, of the latter his greatest bliss: men are as their end is. Here is, 1. Elijah taking leave of his friends, the sons of the prophets, and especially Elisha, who kept close to him, and walked with him through Jordan, ver. 1-10. 2.
2.i: Elisha stayed with Elijah to the end, crossed the Jordan with him, and saw him taken up in a chariot of fire; then Elisha took up his cloak and his work.
2.p: Lord, the God of Elijah is our God too. Give us loyal hearts and show us how to follow You to the end. Amen.
2.l: Tell someone you are not going to leave them, then stay close to them today with a kind word or a helping hand.
q: Elisha asked for a double portion, the heir's share. What do you want to receive from the faith of people who came before you?

3.o: We are now called to attend the public affairs of Israel, in which we shall find Elisha concerned. Here is, I. The general character of Jehoram, king of Israel, ver. 1-3. II. A war with Moab, in which Jehoram and his allies were engaged, ver. 4-8. III. The straits which the confederate army were reduced to in their expedition against Moab, and their consulting Elisha in that distress, with the answer of peace he gave them, ver. 9-19. IV. The glorious issue of this campaign (ver.
3.i: Second Kings 3 is a desert campaign that nearly ends in thirst, until a prophet asks for music and ditches.
3.p: Lord, You send water in the desert. Teach us to trust You enough to dig ditches before the rain. Amen.
3.l: Notice something today that God has provided at just the right moment, and thank Him.
q: A stone buried in Moab agreed with the Bible about a king nobody could check. Where have you found two independent witnesses agreeing?

4.o: Great service Elisha had done, in the foregoing chapter, for the three kings: to his prayers and prophecies they owed their lives and triumphs. One would have expected that the next chapter would tell us what honours and what dignities were conferred on Elisha for this, that he should immediately be preferred at court, and made prime-minister of state, that Jehoshaphat should take him home with him, and advance him in his kingdom. No, the wise man delivered the army, but no man remembered the wise man, Eccl. ix.
4.s: A Room for the Man of God
4.i: A Shunem woman who built a room for Elisha received a promised son, lost him in a sudden illness, and had him restored through Elisha's prayer.
4.p: Lord, You see those who open their homes to Your servants. Bless them, and raise up what we have lost. Amen.
4.l: Prepare a small place for someone today. Tidy your room for a guest, or make a spot for a friend to sit.
q: The woman made room and found her gift. What room could you make for God's work or God's people?

5.o: Two more of Elisha's miracles are recorded in this chapter. I. The cleansing of Naaman, a Syrian, a stranger, from his leprosy, and there, 1. The badness of his case, ver. 1. 2. The providence that brought him to Elisha, the intelligence given him by a captive maid, ver. 2-4. A letter from the king of Syria to the king of Israel, to introduce him, ver. 5-7. And the invitation Elisha sent him, ver. 8. 3. The method prescribed for his cure, his submission, with much ado, to that method, and his cure thereby, ver.
5.s: A Little Girl and a Great Commander
5.i: A captive girl's words lead Naaman to Elisha, and he is healed by washing in the Jordan.
5.p: Lord, You use small voices and simple steps. Humble our pride and heal us as You healed Naaman. Amen.
5.l: Listen today to someone smaller or quieter than you, and take their idea seriously.
q: Naaman almost missed his healing because it was too simple. What simple thing is God asking of you?

6.o: In this chapter we have, I. A further account of the wondrous works of Elisha. 1. His making iron to swim, ver. 1-7. 2. His disclosing to the king of Israel the secret counsels of the king of Syria, ver. 8-12. 3. His saving himself out of the hands of those who were sent to apprehend him, ver. 13-23. II. The besieging of Samaria by the Syrians and the great distress the city was reduced to, ver. 24-33.
6.i: When a borrowed iron axe head fell into the Jordan, Elisha made it float, showing that God cares about small problems and honest people.
6.p: Lord, You care about little things and little people. Make us honest with what is not ours. Amen.
6.l: If you lose or break something that belongs to someone else, tell them honestly and offer to make it right.
q: The man cried that the axe was borrowed. How do you treat things that belong to other people?

7.o: Relief is here brought to Samaria and her king, when the case is, in a manner, desperate, and the king despairing. I. It is foretold by Elisha, and an unbelieving lord shut out from the benefit of it, ver. 1, 2. II. It is brought about, 1. By an unaccountable fright into which God put the Syrians (ver. 6), which caused them to retire precipitately, ver. 7. 2. By the seasonable discovery which four lepers made of this (ver. 3-5), and the account which they gave of it to the court, ver. 8-11. 3.
7.s: Four Men at the Gate of Samaria
7.i: Four hungry outcasts found the enemy camp empty after God scared the Arameans away, and brought good news to the starving city.
7.p: Lord, You use the least expected people to bring good news. Make us ready to share what we have received. Amen.
7.l: If you have good news or something good to share, don't keep it to yourself today. Tell someone.
q: Four outcasts brought the city good news. Who is overlooked around you who might have something to give?

8.o: The passages of story recorded in this chapter oblige us to look back. I. We read before of a Shunammite woman that was a kind benefactor to Elisha; now here we are told how she fared the better for it, afterwards, in the advice Elisha gave her, and the favour the king showed her for his sake, ver. 1-6. II. We read before of the designation of Hazael to be king of Syria (1 Kings xix. 15), and here we have an account of his elevation to that throne and the way he forced for himself to it, by killing his master, ver.
8.i: After seven years of famine in Philistia, the Shunammite woman returned and, just as Gehazi was telling the king of her son's restoration, appealed for her land, and the king restored everything.
8.p: Lord, You care for those who care for Your servants. Thank You for protecting us and for Your perfect timing. Amen.
8.l: Notice a time today when something happens at exactly the right time. Say thank you to God for taking care of you.
q: The woman arrived at exactly the right moment. When has God's timing surprised you?

9.o: Hazael and Jehu were the men that were designed to be the instruments of God's justice in punishing and destroying the house of Ahab. Elijah was told to appoint them to this service; but, upon Ahab's humiliation, a reprieve was granted, and so it was left to Elisha to appoint them.
9.i: Second Kings 9 begins with a flask of oil and ends with the fall of Ahab's house, as Elijah had said.
9.p: Lord, You see every wrong and do not forget it. Keep us from both injustice and from hot-headed vengeance. Amen.
9.l: Remember today that God sees how the powerless are treated, and be kind to someone no one notices.
q: 'Let youth work and age direct.' Who is doing the work in your family or team, and who is directing, and does each know their part?

10.o: We have in this chapter, I. A further account of Jehu's execution of his commission. He cut off, 1. All Ahab's sons, ver. 1-10. 2. All Ahab's kindred, ver. 11-14, 17. 3. Ahab's idolatry: his zeal against this he took Jonadab to be witness to (ver. 15, 16), summoned all the worshippers of Baal to attend (ver. 18-23) and slew them all (ver. 24, 25), and then abolished that idolatry, ver. 26-28. II. A short account of the administration of his government. 1.
10.i: Second Kings 10 is the harshest chapter in Jehu's story: a political and religious purge by a king whose zeal went only part of the way.
10.p: Lord, You want our whole hearts. Search us and show us the idols we keep, and teach us to follow You fully. Amen.
10.l: Look at something you do halfway, and ask God what it would mean to do it with your whole heart.
q: A large family could not protect a house from divine judgment. What do you lean on for security that cannot actually hold?

11.o: The revolution in the kingdom of Israel was soon perfected in Jehu's settlement; we must now enquire into the affairs of the kingdom of Judah, which lost its head (such as it was) at the same time, and by the same hand, as Israel lost its head; but things continued longer there in distraction than in Israel, yet, after some years, they were brought into a good posture, as we find in this chapter. I. Athaliah usurps the government and destroys all the seed-royal, ver. 1. II.
11.i: Second Kings 11 is a rescue and a coup in one chapter: a baby saved from a murderous grandmother, and a priest who crowned him.
11.p: Lord, You preserve what You have promised. Thank You for the people who hide and guard the vulnerable, and bless them. Amen.
11.l: Thank someone today who protected or hid you when you needed it, and tell them what it meant.
q: One queen was building Baal's worship while another king tore it down. What are you building that someone else is tearing down?

12.o: This chapter gives us the history of the reign of Joash, which does not answer to that glorious beginning of it which we had an account of in the foregoing chapter; he was not so illustrious at forty years old as he was at seven, yet his reign is to be reckoned one of the better sort, and appears much worse in Chronicles (2 Chron. xxiv.) than it does here, for there we find the blood of one of God's prophets laid at his door; here we are only told, I. That he did well while Jehoiada lived, ver. 1-3. II.
12.s: A Chest with a Hole in Its Lid
12.i: King Joash has a chest set up in the temple to collect money for repairs, and the workers use it honestly.
12.p: Lord, make us honest and faithful with what You give us, in small things and in large ones. Amen.
12.l: Be honest with money today, even a small amount, and say thank you to someone who is honest with you.
q: Honest handling of money kept the work going. How can you be trusted with something small?

13.o: This chapter brings us again to the history of the kings of Israel, and particularly of the family of Jehu. We have here an account of the reign, I. Of his son Jehoahaz, which continued seventeen years. 1. His bad character in general (ver. 1, 2), the trouble he was brought into (ver. 3), and the low ebb of his affairs, ver. 7. 2. His humiliation before God, and God's compassion towards him, ver. 4, 5, and 23. 3. His continuance in his idolatry notwithstanding, ver. 6. 4. His death, ver. 8, 9. II.
13.i: Elisha's last act was to teach the king that victory belongs to those who give their whole heart, and the king struck the ground only three times.
13.p: Lord, give us hearts that do not stop halfway. Teach us to trust You and to give our whole effort. Amen.
13.l: Do one thing today all the way, with your whole heart, instead of stopping halfway.
q: The king stopped after three strikes. Where are you stopping short of what God offers?

14.o: This chapter continues the history of the succession in the kingdoms both of Judah and Israel. I. In the kingdom of Judah here is, 1. The entire history (as much as is recorded in this book) of Amaziah's reign (1.) His good character, ver. 1-4. (2.) The justice he executed on the murderers of his father, ver. 5, 6. (3.) His victory over the Edomites, ver. 7. (4.) His war with Joash, and his defeat in that war, ver. 8-14. (5.) His fall, at last, by a conspiracy against him, ver. 17-20. 2.
14.i: Second Kings 14 and 15 race across seventy years of kings, with the north in chaos and the south steady but flawed.
14.p: Lord, You humble the proud and lift the lowly. Keep us from pride in our victories, and give us steady hands in unsteady times. Amen.
14.l: Check your pride today: is there a challenge you accepted just to prove you could win?
q: Children must not suffer as guilty for a parent's sin. Where might someone be paying for something that was never theirs?

15.o: In this chapter, I. The history of two of the kings of Judah is briefly recorded:—1. Of Azariah, or Uzziah, ver. 1-7. 2. Of Jotham his son, ver. 32-38. II. The history of many of the kings of Israel that reigned at the same time is given us in short, five in succession, all of whom, except one, went down slain to the pit, and their murders were their successors. 1. Zachariah, the last of the house of Jehu, reigned six months, and then was slain and succeeded by Shallum, ver. 8-12. 2.
15.i: Second Kings 14 and 15 race across seventy years of kings, with the north in chaos and the south steady but flawed.
15.p: Lord, You humble the proud and lift the lowly. Keep us from pride in our victories, and give us steady hands in unsteady times. Amen.
15.l: Check your pride today: is there a challenge you accepted just to prove you could win?
q: Children must not suffer as guilty for a parent's sin. Where might someone be paying for something that was never theirs?

16.o: This chapter is wholly taken up with the reign of Ahaz; and we have quite enough of it, unless it were better. He had a good father, and a better son, and yet was himself one of the worst of the kings of Judah. I. He was a notorious idolater, ver. 1-4. II. With the treasures of the temple, as well as his own, he hired the king of Assyria to invade Syria and Israel, ver. 5-9. III. He took pattern from an idol's altar which he saw at Damascus for a new altar in God's temple, ver. 10-16. IV.
16.s: Ahaz's Altar and the Fall of Samaria
16.i: Second Kings 16 and 17 show a king in Judah who borrowed an altar and a kingdom in the north that was lost, all for the same reason.
16.p: Lord, we trust You, not empires or altars. Keep us from half-hearted loyalty, and bring back those who are far away. Amen.
16.l: Choose today to trust God rather than a powerful friend or a clever plan.
q: Where are you tempted to fix a mistake with a worse shortcut?

17.o: This chapter gives us an account of the captivity of the ten tribes, and so finishes the history of that kingdom, after it had continued about 265 years, from the setting up of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. In it we have, I. A short narrative of this destruction, ver. 1-6. II. Remarks upon it, and the causes of it, for the justifying of God in it and for warning to others, ver. 7-23. III. An account of the nations which succeeded them in the possession of their land, and the mongrel religion set up among them, ver.
17.s: Ahaz's Altar and the Fall of Samaria
17.i: Second Kings 16 and 17 show a king in Judah who borrowed an altar and a kingdom in the north that was lost, all for the same reason.
17.p: Lord, we trust You, not empires or altars. Keep us from half-hearted loyalty, and bring back those who are far away. Amen.
17.l: Choose today to trust God rather than a powerful friend or a clever plan.
q: Where are you tempted to fix a mistake with a worse shortcut?

18.o: When the prophet had condemned Ephraim for lies and deceit he comforted himself with this, that Judah yet "ruled with God, and was faithful with the Most Holy," Hos. xi. 12. It was a very melancholy view which the last chapter gave us of the desolations of Israel; but this chapter shows us the affairs of Judah in a good posture at the same time, that it may appear God has not quite cast off the seed of Abraham, Rom. xi. 1. Hezekiah is here upon the throne, I. Reforming his kingdom, ver. 1-6. II.
18.i: Second Kings 18 and 19 show a king threatened by the greatest army of his day, and what he did with the threat.
18.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of Your people when the world is loud. Help us to bring our fears to You first. Amen.
18.l: When something frightens you today, stop and tell God about it first, before you tell anyone else.
q: All three of Rabshakeh's suggestions were false. Which discouraging voice have you listened to that sounded reasonable?

19.o: Jerusalem's great distress we read of in the foregoing chapter, and left it besieged, insulted, threatened, terrified, and just ready to be swallowed up by the Assyrian army. But in this chapter we have an account of its glorious deliverance, not by sword or bow, but by prayer and prophecy, and by the hand of an angel. I. Hezekiah, in great concern, sent to the prophet Isaiah, to desire his prayers (ver. 1-5) and received from him an answer of peace, ver. 6, 7. II.
19.i: Second Kings 18 and 19 show a king threatened by the greatest army of his day, and what he did with the threat.
19.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of Your people when the world is loud. Help us to bring our fears to You first. Amen.
19.l: When something frightens you today, stop and tell God about it first, before you tell anyone else.
q: All three of Rabshakeh's suggestions were false. Which discouraging voice have you listened to that sounded reasonable?

20.o: In this chapter we have, I. Hezekiah's sickness, and his recovery from that, in answer to prayer, in performance of a promise, in the use of means, and confirmed with a sign, ver. 1-11. II. Hezekiah's sin, and his recovery from that, ver. 12-19. In both of these, Isaiah was God's messenger to him. III. The conclusion of his reign, ver. 20, 21.
20.i: God tells Hezekiah he will die, hears his prayer, and adds fifteen years, with a shadow moving back on the stairway.
20.p: Lord, You number our days. Teach us to use them well, and to trust You with our lives. Amen.
20.l: Pray for someone who is sick today, and ask God to heal them.
q: Hezekiah asked for more life and God gave it. How would you use fifteen more years?

21.o: In this chapter we have a short but sad account of the reigns of two of the kings of Judah, Manasseh and Amon. I. Concerning Manasseh, all the account we have of him here is, 1. That he devoted himself to sin, to all manner of wickedness, idolatry, and murder, ver. 1-9 and 16. 2. That therefore God devoted him, and Jerusalem for his sake, to ruin, ver. 10-18. In the book of Chronicles we have an account of his troubles, and his repentance. II. Concerning Amon we are only told that he lived in sin (ver.
21.i: Second Kings 21 tells of the longest and worst reign in Judah, and sets up the verdict that Jerusalem will fall.
21.p: Lord, You are patient even with the worst of us. Keep us from following bad examples, and hear the prayer of those who humble themselves. Amen.
21.l: If you have done something wrong, ask God to forgive you today, and believe He hears.
q: Israel stood on good terms with God and still would not listen. What advantage have you been given that you are not using?

22.o: This chapter begins the story of the reign of good king Josiah, whose goodness shines the brighter because it came just after so much wickedness, which he had the honour to reform, and just before so great a destruction, which yet he had not the honour to prevent. Here, after his general character (ver. 1, 2), we have a particular account of the respect he paid I. To God's house, which he repaired, ver. 3-7 II. To God's book, which he was much affected with the reading of, ver. 8-11 III.
22.s: The Book Found in the Temple
22.i: While repairing the temple, workers find the Book of the Law, and young King Josiah is moved to tears and to action.
22.p: Lord, give us tender hearts that listen to Your Word and obey it. Amen.
22.l: Read a part of the Bible today, and ask God to help you obey what it says.
q: Josiah's heart was tender when he heard God's Word. How do you respond when you read the Bible?

23.o: We have here, I. The happy continuance of the goodness of Josiah's reign, and the progress of the reformation he began, reading the law (ver. 1, 2), renewing the covenant (ver. 3), cleansing the temple (ver. 4), and rooting out idols and idolatry, with all the relics thereof, in all places, as far as his power reached (ver. 5-20), keeping a solemn passover (ver. 21-23), and clearing the country of witches (ver. 24); and in all this acting with extraordinary vigour, ver. 25 II.
23.s: The King Reads the Whole Book
23.i: King Josiah read the rediscovered Book of the Law to the whole people, renewed God's covenant, and tore down idols throughout Judah.
23.p: Lord, give us hearts that tremble at Your word and hands that obey it. Amen.
23.l: Read part of your Bible out loud today, even a few verses, to yourself or someone else.
q: Josiah had been quietly clearing away idols for years before the book was found. What good work are you already doing that you have not yet formally promised?

24.o: Things are here ripening for, and hastening towards, the utter destruction of Jerusalem. We left Jehoiakim on the throne, placed there by the king of Egypt: now here we have, I. The troubles of his reign, how he was brought into subjection by the king of Babylon, and severely chastised for attempting to shake off the yoke (ver. 1-6), and how Egypt also was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar, ver. 7. II.
24.i: Second Kings 24 records the first deportation to Babylon, the beginning of the end for the kingdom of Judah.
24.p: Lord, You are with Your people in exile. Bring comfort to those who have lost their homes, and teach us to trust You when everything shakes. Amen.
24.l: Pray today for people who have had to leave their homes, and ask God to give them a new place to belong.
q: They set up kings but not by God. Whose leadership have you chosen without asking him?

25.o: Ever since David's time Jerusalem had been a celebrated place, beautiful for situation and the joy of the whole earth: while the book of psalms lasts that name will sound great. In the New Testament we read much of it, when it was, as here, ripening again for its ruin. In the close of the Bible we read of a new Jerusalem. Every thing therefore that concerns Jerusalem is worthy our regard. In this chapter we have, I. The utter destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, the city besieged and taken (ver.
25.i: After a long siege, Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple and took most of its people to Babylon, but God's promises to His people continued.
25.p: Lord, You are faithful even when everything is lost. Keep our hope in You when the walls fall. Amen.
25.l: Be gentle today with someone who is grieving something they have lost. Sit with them, or send a note.
q: Judah lost its city, its temple and its king. What do you hold most tightly that you would still have if everything else were taken?
